utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. The affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. My name is Borivoje Borovic, I am the Defence counsel of Miroslav Radic. My first question, before you left for Vukovar did you know what the reason was for the JNA stepping in to resolve matters in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind as to share that with us?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason for them going there was the emergence of armed units that were holding Vukovar under their control unlawfully, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear at the time that this had anything to do with the Vukovar barracks?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a frequent occurrence at the time. JNA barracks, throughout Croatia, were coming under siege by armed civilians, and the army frequently had difficulties securing the barracks and evacuating their soldiers, and this was one of those cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When did you find out about that? Before you left that day to conduct the interview or was it much earlier when the JNA intervention will originally begun?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was much earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I have your statement to the OTP in front of you, I also have the interview, so if there is any need to read out any portions, I can help you with that, or do you have copies already?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified yesterday that you were taking pictures of dead bodies near the hospital. At one point there was a soldier who stood in the way, but after the situation was resolved, that's at least what you said, and you were eventually able to take your photographs. Does that mean that at the time when you were taking photographs of buildings and people there was nobody, no soldier standing in your way, you were perfectly free to do what you wanted at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday on page 7289 of the transcript, lines 9 through 11, you stated that before you started your interview with Mr. Radic in that half-ruined house the army had begun to leave Vukovar on that day, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And that is the reason why you spent nearly one and a half hours waiting for Radic to appear in that house?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: He just came to say good-bye, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Before you started your interview you had said that Radic was a well-respected officer of the JNA, and you were recommended him to interview of all people, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In addition to telling you that he was a well-respected officer, did they say he was brave too? Did they say he required discipline, that he was a responsible officer, what else did they tell you about Mr. Radic before you conducted this interview?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was something along these lines: That was the general impression, I can't really remember specifically but I was told that he was a well-respected, model officer of the JNA and this was the reason I was to meet him and interview him of all people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the interview that you made there is some reference to this, and that is my question. During your interview, did you learn that he was against robbery, against looting, against killing, that he had sent home over 40 volunteers just to keep them from doing things like those? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. My interview reflects that, doesn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What was your impression that this was indeed how he acted how he behaved during the war operations?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my impression, he left a very good, very favourable impression on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you be so kind as to tell us who briefed you on how you should conduct your interview with Radic, what you were to ask him about, what you were to ask him about his actions at the front line?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think anybody did that. But I can't be certain now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, before you started your interview did you know exactly what post he was holding in the JNA at that point in time, and during the operations in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know. I learned in the middle of the interview. I'm not sure if he told me himself or other people who were there, but I had not previously been aware of his exact post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So you found out he was commander of one of the JNA companies there, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Likewise, you described yesterday that damaged tank that you saw on Petrova Gora. My question is, in addition to that, did you see any ruined or damaged buildings in the same area where the house was, where you conducted your interview?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were some damaged buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you provide a closer description of those?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean a closer description? There are details I don't remember. What is certain is that all or most of the houses at any rate were damaged. I think all, in fact, there wasn't a single house that was virtually intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What about those people who were present during your interview, did they tell you anything about who caused that damage, members of the ZNG, another armed unit or whatever, what did they call them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody told me anything about who had done that, nothing at all was said about that. The term used in reference to the other side, the enemy, were for the most part ZNG and Ustashas. Those were the two terms being used predominantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you conduct any sort of conversation at all in addition to what you told us yesterday about those Croatian paramilitary units we have just heard what the terms being used were. Where were their main defence lines? What well-known features did they occupy at the time, did you learn anything about that while you were there? More specifically, did they tell you anything about snipers, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were things being said about snipers, but in addition to all the information that I published, I can hardly be expected to remember any other details. This was, after all, 15 years ago, and there were references to snipers, there were references to where exactly the Croatian defence forces were, where their strongholds were, where their positions were, but I can't remember any details about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you remember in relation to these snipers, did anyone mention the archers club, the marksman's club in Vukovar, were most of those snipers members of that club?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, somebody did drop a hint to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear not only during the interview, but also during your time in the area, or later for that matter because you did go to Vukovar later on, that in addition to the ZNG and the police forces back in 1991 there were members of the HOS, and paramilitary units, that came from somewhere abroad, that there were a lot of foreigners fighting on the Croatian side. Did you hear that in Vukovar a lot of volunteers from all parts of Croatia had assembled?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found out about the foreigners and about volunteers from other towns. I imagined to interview a couple of those foreigners later on at the Mitrovica prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you tell us more about that, please? Those foreigners, which specific countries did they come from, how did they arrive in Vukovar, what did you, as an investigating journalist, find out about that at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had occasion to interview one American and one Dutch person who were captured around Vukovar and they both said that they were adventurers who just arrived in the area of their own accord, nobody had helped them to get there and it was based on their personal convictions that they took sides and that was all I could glean from what they told me. That was all I learned about the reasons for their arrival in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you perhaps know that they were mercenaries, that they were foreign mercenaries, that they were being paid for being there and fighting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know a thing or two about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm about to ask you something about a person that yesterday you referred to as Stuka, or Pike. Do you know what that person's real name is without reading and checking?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His surname is Petkovic, I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Yesterday you talked about conducting the interview in that half-ruined building and you said that somewhere nearby one of your fellow journalists was interviewing Stuka. My question is, does that mean that you did not see Stuka on that day?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain, sir, since you testified yesterday, both in chief and in cross-examination, that he came at least once to your offices, the offices of your newspaper. Can you tell me exactly who he came there to see?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know specifically who he was there to see, but whoever it was that he had been interviewed by.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Which year was that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in late 1991 or possibly early 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How do you know that if you are certain that he didn't talk to you, that Stuka had been there and why was it so important for you to be told and for you to now tell us specifically? Did he come to you and ask you to write about him or was it for a different reason? Can you please try to think back and try to remember?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact reason for him being there. Somebody did tell me that he was there and that's what I remember. But that's all I knew about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 7304 of the transcript, lines 17 through 19, you said that you went to Vukovar two or three times after the war or after the liberation of Vukovar. The reason being you hosted delegations of foreign journalists there, as well as representatives of various political institutions just to show them around, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question is, in what official capacity did you take representatives of foreign international institutions there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was externally contracted to a Serbian company, and these people were in touch with someone in the States and they brought those people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which company? I don't think that should be very harmful if you tell us, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's called ABC Produkt that's what it's called.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Were you manager or an editor-in-chief with that company at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Later on, after those rounds of Vukovar. It was later on, sometime in 1995, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What exactly did that company do, what sort of activity did that company pursue, ABC Produkt, before you took over? What did they do?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the beginning of the 1990s it dealt in transport, trade, and printing. Those were their three principal areas of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So why was this company suddenly interested in going to Vukovar and in checking what had been going on during the war, this political delegation, I mean?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is because this company organised the arrival of those people from America, so they planned their stay there, they drew up the schedule and this schedule included a visit to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about which political delegation this was? What was the name of this political delegation and how many times did you take them to Vukovar and did they pay you for that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an informal delegation comprising several officials who had introduced themselves as being attached to the offices of several different congressmen in the States, as well as a handful of journalists, journalists from the Voice of America and another paper. They didn't pay me for that, they just paid for the expenses but nothing in addition to that. There was no additional fee.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Have you ever heard of a journalist named Jovan Dulovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was he working with these political organisations at the same time too, the ones you took to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And who was he working with then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would really be hard put to say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know a journalist named Tomasevic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was he working with these political organisations that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think anybody else was attached to them. They arrived in a different way. Their interest was obvious, but it was equally obvious that they knew no one there, and that they knew little about the situation if anything. I don't think they had any other contacts, save for those that I've specified.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You also testified yesterday, or rather you pointed out for our benefit the Danube Hotel, which was a symbol of the town that had been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a landmark, and everybody tended to notice it somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: If I told you that the so-called Danube platoon a paramilitary unit and its command were positioned or stationed in the hotel ever since January 1991, that there were many foreigners there wearing uniforms, perhaps if you think back to the time you spent at Petrova Gora, do you remember anybody there telling you anything about the Ustashas being in control of the Danube Hotel all the time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was a well-known fact. I didn't verify that, but it was a well-known fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So you agree with me, what I have just put to you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In October and November, 1991, do you know if there was newspaper being published in Serbia called Ekspres Politika?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't get the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: At that time in 1991 -- my apologies. It's for the transcript, the interpreter failed to hear your answer and your answer was, "Yes," right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At that time back in 1991 this newspaper, Ekspres Politika, did it serve the needs of the regime, if you know that what means? Did it toady up to the regime?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know what that means and you could say that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Who was in power in Serbia at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Socialist Party of Serbia. And the president of that party was Serbia's president too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And the name is?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say you have heard of Jovan Dulovic. Do you know that he was Ekspres Politika's reporter from the Vukovar front at the time? Is this something you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So he was writing for this pro-regime newspaper, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Aleksandar Vasiljevic is?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What can you tell us about him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is a JNA general, he was at one time the head of the counter-intelligence services.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about whether he interfered with the newspaper's policies in terms of how the army was being reported on?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have nothing reliable about that. People were saying all sorts of things. I knew that he was well-connected in a number of editors' offices? A wide range of newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Such as?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some journalists were given informal chances to meet with him and talk to him, such as the journalists of the Nin [Realtime transcript read in error "Knin"] newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he was well-connected with Ekspres Politika who were covering the war in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: At the time, you mean.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is an error in the transcript. It says the Knin newspaper whereas it should read the Nin newspaper, N-i-n, if that can be corrected, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: This article about Miroslav Radic, what is the headline of that interview?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Disgusted of the war," that's how it reads. "I have grown disgusted with the war."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you involved in making this the headline for this article? Please go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was behind this head line.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please now look at the interview and try to find the second question you asked Radic, which was, "What was the fighting that you took part in like?" Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the first two passages for us, what Captain Miroslav Radic stated in this interview? Please read slowly, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The first few days we encountered extremely heavy resistance from our opponents. They had been preparing for the fight for months before we arrived. They expected the army to attack, so they dug in and made underground tunnels so that they could move between shelters and fortifications. They camouflaged themselves well and it was difficult to spot them. This was my first experience of combat."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you slow down a little, please?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "This was my first experience of this sort of combat. I had knowledge but experience is something altogether different."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified in chief yesterday about the first two passages that's the last question, and the last question is, "Today, as you leave Vukovar, what is the most important lesson you have learned during the fighting?" It's not going to be long. Please don't read the first two paragraphs that you read out yesterday, but paragraphs number 3, 4, and 5. And that also concludes my cross-examination, I'm sure the Chamber will be happy to hear.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The one who started this war and who stirred up clashes between the peoples, because this amounted almost to a war of religion between the Orthodox and the Catholic peoples, whoever started that should be placed right in the middle and beaten from both sides. "I don't know whether there is any point in sending out an appeal because I don't know whether that would be doable or not, but no war regardless of its nature, with the possible exception of the wars of liberation, can ever bring luck to anybody. Mothers, women, and children must mourn. I saw one of my reservists who had been killed. He left behind three children, the eldest of whom was not older than eight years the question is what he had to die for. Just for whose ideas or fantasies. It wasn't just him. There were many people like that. "This matter should be resolved by political means and through negotiations. Anything is better than war. Nevertheless, there is something that lurks in every human being. I'm not sure what it is. I've grown disgusted with this war. I wouldn't wish it upon anybody to be in the same kind of situation as we have spent the past two months in. This story is difficult to tell or explain. It's an experience that goes on and on. None of my dreams were about my family, my children, my parents, or my peacetime existence. Even in my dreams all I have been worrying about is the army. It is an obsession. It is a heavy burden, and it is hard to get rid of it. I don't know how I will behave once I am back in Belgrade."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this is a fitting end to my cross-examination. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all. Good morning, Mr. Kacarevic, my name is Novak Lukic, attorney-at-law. I'll be asking you questions on behalf of Veselin Sljivancanin's defence team. Please bear in mind the fact that we speak in the same language and there needs to be interpretation. So please pause between my questions and your answers. Most of my questions will be -- will require yes or no answers. If any further clarification needs to be provided, you can certainly say so. You confirmed yesterday that you were a journalist with the newspaper known as Intervju at the time relevant for this Court. Did you have a special area that you covered in terms of what the general nature of that newspaper was, which was interviewing celebrities, famous people?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We tried to do everything, we tried to cover everything. For the most part I covered economics and politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You testified that you were a journalist at the time. However, I came across information indicating that you were a member of the Collegium?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I was a member of the board. Which means that I was kind of an editor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: About the Vukovar operations we know this went on until mid-November. Was there anyone in your newspaper who spent this whole time at the front line in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several people from our newspaper who sent in reports from the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But as far as I can tell each and every issue of your magazine brought something that was interesting for your readers and that was in relation to the Vukovar front?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if each and every issue, but we did cover that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you in touch with other fellow journalists from other magazines, journals and newspapers who went to the Vukovar front to cover what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was in touch with other journalists, and we exchanged information, we exchanged verified and unverified information alike, and there were all sorts of things being said about this at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you in a position to follow what the media abroad were saying about Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not very often. We only were able to follow any foreign media in as far as this was being reported in our domestic media. We could follow a situation in Vukovar, but there wasn't that much being published, especially not in Slavonia itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that there was a special focus over the last few days of the fighting and after the liberation from mid-November onwards?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. The interest in Vukovar grew as the fighting was drawing to a close.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that at that time, perhaps even on the 19th of November, there was a sensational piece of news, an Italian agency reported that over 40 dead bodies of children had been found in an orphanage. Do you remember this making head-lines in those days?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I remember that. I think this is still much debated, and I think there are probably court cases and libel cases to ascertain whether that was false or not. People are still dragging this through courtrooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is especially true of our own domestic media, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of November do you remember Cyrus Vance, personal envoy of the Secretary-General of the United Nations visiting Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. Now that you've jogged my memory, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this as a professional journalist. We've heard testimony before this Court that Sljivancanin pointed a rifle at Cyrus Vance in a bid to prevent him from approaching the hospital. Do you think this would make for an attractive headline? What is your view as a journalist, since journalists were in the area covering it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think this happened. First I hear of it. If this was true, it certainly would have been impossible to conceal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the JNA made it possible for a certain media at the time, even foreign media, to do some front line reporting, such media as Sky News, as an example?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that, but I'm not familiar with any details. I know there were attempts to secure access for foreign media, even more so than for domestic media to prevent any erroneous reports from coming out, but I don't know about Sky News or any foreign media specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My learned friend, Mr. Domazet, asked you a number of questions about the relationship between the authorities and the media. I understand that at the time the authorities were trying to keep the media under control in the sense of interfering with their staffing policies. That was my understanding of what you testified?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this would be the briefest possible description of how they tried to exercise control over the work of the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In actual fact the less interference with the authorities there was, the freer the media were, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That seems like a fair assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You testified yesterday briefly about the bi-weekly, Intervju. You were trying to interview celebrities who your editors thought might interest the general public. Who was the founder of this paper?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Politika newspaper company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So Intervju was one of Politika's publications, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Zika Milanic [as interpreted], does that ring a bell? Who was he?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time he was the editor-in-chief of the daily Politika, and the manager of the entire company, or enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Correction for the transcript, Zika Minovic, M-i-n-o-v-i-c. You will agree with me that at the time he -- this person was believed to be a -- a fervent follower of Slobodan Milosevic and his policies, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The editor-in-chief of Intervju at the time was a man named Petar Jankovic, right? That's what my information suggests.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he had been appointed editor-in-chief, just several months earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Dragan Vlahovic, wasn't he the deputy editor-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. He used to be editor-in-chief, but then a new one appointed and he became the new deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dragan Vlahovic is a name you had mentioned as one of the people who were with you in Vukovar, the group that comprised three journalists and photo reporters, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if your core staff was informed at the time, or did you personally hear that on the 21st of November the federal secretariat for All People's Defence, or their information office organised a huge press conference and that the journalists were given a chance to tour the Vukovar area? Is this something you remember, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand, you became interested, your newspaper became interested, after the footage showing the clash between Mr. Sljivancanin and Mr. Borsinger, the International Committee of the Red Cross man in Vukovar was shown, the clash that occurred on 20th of November, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I can have the OTP's assistance on this, please, I would like now to show again the footage that we've already seen so many times. This is Exhibit 318. Mr. Kacarevic, we're about to see a short video clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kacarevic, is that the famous footage that you mentioned yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who do you recognise?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin and Colonel Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just what I was about to ask, if you could see any other officers apart from Mr. Sljivancanin. And your answer Colonel Nebojsa Pavkovic, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have information to indicate, but I believe you can actually see that if you look at the date of the recording, or rather can you tell me which TV station this footage or video clip was taken from, have you noticed that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have information to indicate this was actually broadcast on the 20th of November on the evening news. Let me ask you something else: Do you remember if, at the time, TV Belgrade would show so-called additional news after the regular evening news?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was this additional news programme about? What constituted the general nature of that programme, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking it was used for propaganda. They had a different topic every time, but at the time it was mostly about the spreading clashes. It was about the fighting, it was about the fate of the refugees. It was about the confessions of survivors, people who survived the horrors of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say it was used for propaganda, mostly. For the benefit of the Chamber, I believe we more or less agree under whose control, or under whose influence was TV Belgrade at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: TV Belgrade was under the direct influence of the party in power at the time, the influence of Slobodan Milosevic, and his closest allies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This additional news programme, perhaps you will remember, sometimes it went on for a very long time depending on the viewers' interest. Sometimes they would go on from 8.00 in the evening until 11.00, there were no major restrictions placed on that programme?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In relation to the footage that we've just seen, what do you remember about the reaction of the public in Serbia at the time when this was shown on TV? I mean the media and the -- those involved in politics?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My basic impression is that this footage was very much in the public eye. Everybody seems to have seen it, and suddenly Sljivancanin became a celebrity because of this footage that was shown. Most of the public looked favourably on Sljivancanin's role as it was portrayed in this footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we now go back for a while to November, 1991, and the autumn of 1991 in general. Will you agree with me if I say at the time the media in Serbia in general, especially those who were under the influence of the party in power, were not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the counsel please repeat the last part of the question? The interpreter did not get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will have to repeat the last part of my question. I apologise to the interpreters. My question is, at the time the media in Serbia did not portray the international institutions in a favourable light, or various intergovernmental organisations, the predominant reason being the way these institutions and organisations viewed the conflict in Yugoslavia and from the positions of our own political party's organisations. I'm not sure if you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes, you could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that, and I'm talking about those involved in politics now, there was a certain degree of animosity towards the way the international media were covering the JNA and the role of the JNA in the break-up of the former Yugoslavia, and the same sort of animosity was felt towards coverage by most of the international observers in the area at the time, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was a time when our public was just beginning to familiarise itself with the simplified way in which events in our country were being shown. Everything was being portrayed very much in black and white, and reality was never that simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As a media professional, can you tell me something about this, this propaganda, this propaganda in the media, was this something that was organised or something that was very much erratic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean our media, it was quite spontaneous and very often counter-productive. As for international media, I don't know. They seemed better organised at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you saw this footage with Sljivancanin, and the other times that he appeared on television, was it your impression, and this is more or less what you did say yesterday so I'm asking you more specifically today, that this was a different JNA officer in respect of how the JNA had communicated with the public until that point very clearly, in a very clear-cut fashion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, there are several explanations why Sljivancanin attracted so much public attention at that time, and what you have just said is among those reasons. As I said, this was the first officer who appeared in this role, not a desk officer, just issuing communications from his office and statements in writing, but he was in the public eye and people who would see him in the flesh, an officer in Vukovar. And then he talked about a topic which was really very much preoccupying the public, the organisation of all factors relevant to the conflict in Vukovar, the organisations featuring in the conflict in Vukovar, and he said something which was very much shared by the rest of the public, and this is what markedly heightened his popularity in the public eye.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Am I wrong if I say that the media and the public needed to pin-point a hero after this so to speak, victory, who would be materialised and that Sljivancanin was indeed the ideal person for that role?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what the reaction was among your own colleagues in your editorial office after you saw this footage and prior to your departure for Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this footage elicited the comments all over the place, and everybody talked about it. These reactions, first of all, were the undivided attention of everybody, and we assessed that it would be advisable for us to acquaint the public with this person in more detail, because everybody had found about the existence of Sljivancanin at that particular point, but not really what he was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In relation to this footage, do you also perhaps remember this footage having been shown on our television later which was on that -- of course the television under the influence of the party in power, which showed the relationship of the international community towards the JNA and how they saw its role in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that that footage was shown on our television countless times, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We shall also talk about the interview later, but let me just clarify one thing. From talking with him, both in that interview and later as well, and you did say that you had later contacts with him, did you gain the impression that Sljivancanin was a person who wanted to speak about all questions asked him openly? Did you gain that impression, that he wanted that talk openly, especially with the media representatives?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from our very first encounter it was my impression that he was a very frank person, a person completely open to the interests of the profession that I pursued, because actually given his line of -- his profession, because prior to that we always had difficulties with representatives of the JNA, it was always associated with some permits and what have you, and it was practically virtually impossible to be granted interviews. And Sljivancanin, from our very first meeting, actually showed a most uncustomary openness to discuss all topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With relation to the actual content of the text, including this particular dialogue, were you interested at that time to further investigate his words from the bridge? "This evening my soldiers also got killed. This evening my soldiers also got killed this evening." Did that prompt you to write something about it or to investigate that statement further?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I believe that we talked about it, but it was not included in my text. I cannot recall the details. We did, however, discuss the topic, but I can't be sure of my memory right now. I cannot rely on it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is a small part of the text which refers to that, but I was asking in principle, generally after that, were you interested in pursuing that topic further? Were you also interested in hearing the other side, to hear what the reaction was of the International Red Cross and whether there were any statements issued in connection with that conflict from the International Red Cross, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not remember what happened further in connection with this controversial case. I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The then attitude, the then position of your paper was not that you should perhaps establish contact with a representative of the Red Cross and conduct a talk with them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps, yes. Perhaps they did think that it would be necessary, but I cannot remember at this point. When we speak today about it, it is quite logical, it stands to reason that we also sought to hear the other side, but I cannot remember now, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But at that particular moment when you saw that footage and in your editor's office decided that you should seek out this person in Vukovar, which was designated by your side and by your paper as the Knight from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you, not you personally, but the editor-in-chief, I suppose, in view of the importance of the entire topic you decided that he should feature on the cover of that particular issue where the interview was published, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would I be wrong if I said that -- if I claimed that your desire to have as soon as possible, namely that evening, when the brigade arrived in Belgrade, as you said it was on the 24th of November in the evening, to have that interview with him conducted so as to gain an edge over some other competitive papers concretely speaking the Nin magazine, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Sljivancanin did not only elicit our attention, because given these competitive relations, we had a handicap interview that we were fortnightly bi-weekly and the issue, the dead-line for completing our issue was a Monday, for inserting any text into that particular issue and that was why we were in such a hurry to complete this task by that dead-line and we were aware of the fact that other papers were also trying to do the same, and that was of course an additional problem that we had to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that interview and the cover page of the magazine Intervju, as well as these other articles that we discussed were actually published in the 29th of November, 1991, the anniversary issue of Intervju, were they not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please just take a brief look at this article of the Intervju of Sljivancanin, which is called, "The return of the -- return of a warrior." I suppose that these two first paragraphs before the actual question, the first question is a text, an introductory text by you why you decided to interview him and where you found him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And there you note in the very first paragraph, that he had become -- he had certainly become one of the most well-known officers of the JNA, thanks to TV reports from the battle front, which portrayed him as an excellent soldier, and a resolute officer. This conclusion of yours was given, namely on the basis of the footage on the basis of which you actually established your view of him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you retain that impression after you had met him in person, and after you had conducted your interview with him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you gain the impression from talking to him that he was sincerely affected by the devastation of the city and the perishing of so many civilians in it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you gain the impression from talking to him that he was proud because the Yugoslav People's Army was a multi-national one, and that is, in fact, indicated in the text? Did you gain that impression, that that was the case, that he was proud of that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time Sljivancanin quite frankly and candidly advocated the idea of brotherhood and unity. He bore the symbols, the emblems of the Yugoslav People's Army that had already started to be substituted. He still wore the five-pointed star, and he struck one as a man who did so with conviction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This five-pointed star symbol, it was a symbol of the flag of the SFRY, was already anachronous at that time even in relation to positions maintained within the JNA, it was not that popular within the JNA ranks, and generally a pro-Yugoslav position, pro-Yugoslav partial -- was not all that popular at that time, was it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the other side in Vukovar had its own star with its own symbols of the Independent State of Croatia from the Second World War, which show the particular unrest and fear among the population, but as far as the Yugoslav People's Army is concerned, those symbols were also quite compromised, there were some volunteers and other members who did not want to bear such symbols anymore, but just wanted to wear their own emblems and did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask the secretary -- the registry, and would like to thank the registry on this occasion for so expeditiously helping us in preparing the electronic version. There is 3D01-0062 and we shall of course put a question in regard to the witness. Yesterday, actually, I informed the Prosecutor of that document; I believe that there will no problem for us to hear a comment on it. Mr. Kacarevic, can you tell us what it is that we can see on our screens today -- now, sorry.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the cover page of the magazine Intervju, the issue in which the talk with Sljivancanin was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should have been taken that evening when we actually conducted the interview, which is to say on the 20th -- in the evening -- on the 24th of November in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The 20th of November, 1991 was still the day of the republic officially --

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 29th, you mean, of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you read the head line in the -- in red, in red letters?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that is the announcement of the interview, on the cover page it says, "Veselin Sljivancanin, the Knight from Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you see this emblem? First of all, can you tell us what is the emblem, what is written on it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this is a patch which is actually the Yugoslav flag, or the flag of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia with a five-pointed star and it is indicated above that it is SFRY, or the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether this patch was worn by many officers when you were in Vukovar by many officers and men when you were in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. There really were many different uniforms and we encountered at least -- the fewest officers and there so many different uniforms and so many different patches I can't really remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From what I read in the introductory part of your text, I see that you actually talked to him and you could see, you say here that there were still some things lying about, strewn about, a military belt, et cetera, did you get the impression that he had just arrived from the battle front?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is why I wrote so. That was my impression. And I believe that it was a correct one, that Major Sljivancanin had just arrived in Belgrade, and half an hour after that we came to see him and the conducted in the interview. In the room where we talked there were obvious traces of someone having arrived only recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to propose that this photograph be tendered into evidence, if the Prosecution has no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: No observation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number 358.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is that a convenient time? Or are you very near?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I certainly have a number of other questions, not too many, but I should like to wrap up this particular topic by another couple of questions, and then we can make the break. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday to the Prosecutor that you remembered how Sljivancanin had helped you when you were the first who entered the White Palace. Would you explain for the distinguished Chamber, what is this White Palace, whose residence was it prior to your entry, and why couldn't one gain access to it, and whose residence was it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to the Second World War, this was the royal house of the Karadjordjevic Dynasty, and after the war, the white palace was used ass the residence of the Yugoslav Marshal, Josip Broz Tito. So for a very long time it was one of the secretive edifices about which rumours could be heard but very few had occasion to actually see from the inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said before the war that was before the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, prior to the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another -- just one more question and we shall finish with this topic. Do you remember, did you ever gain any information as to the attitude, as to the feeling of Mr. Sljivancanin towards Josip Broz Tito?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could only say something from my memory, but I believe that he harboured a negative position in this regard, if I'm sure -- but I'm not sure, I cannot be sure at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can take that break now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's occurring to me, Mr. Lukic, we either have three very short sessions today, or we have two full-length, and finish a little early. Because of the late start we can't have three sessions of the normal time. Would it be more practical to have full-length sessions and finish early, do you think? I see some support on the faces of those around. In that event, you could carry on now and finish your questioning of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I still have about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Keep going.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Kacarevic, now we shall deal with the actual interview with Mr. Sljivancanin, from what I -- what I can see from the text, you asked -- put to him five questions, I counted them, and the basic topic of the interview was actually the conflict, the argument between Sljivancanin and the Red Cross representatives, and this was the focus of your attention; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You had been in Vukovar prior to that interview and you had seen everything that you have already described for us. Part of your impression -- impressions is also shown on these photographs. I'm not sure whether you have that section with the photographs that you published along with the interview, these two pages of black and white -- white photographs. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do have it, but it is a poor image of -- of course, I know what they are about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me just read this comment, and I suppose it is an editorial comment accompanying these photographs. I'm reading the text, and please, you follow whether I'm doing it right. "The journalist of interview found themselves the only people in Vukovar last week in several yards across from the Vukovar Hospital when JNA members were taking care of the bodies of 93 innocent victims of Ustasha terror. With understanding shown on the part of the -- of the army -- army officers they -- the journalist made attempts of photographs of the perished children, women, and old people." Let me ask you, the victims of Ustasha terror. Was this term, the "Ustasha terror," something that was customary to designate at that time, the other side?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was quite customary. In fact, the Croatian armed formations -- armed units called themselves that very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did anyone prevent you from talking, try to forbid you from talking to anyone in Vukovar whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We heard from your statement that you were led through the city up to this point near the hospital by a local who knew the streets and that you took some side streets, that entire streets were virtually impassable, and did I understand you well that these officers who were surprised of your presence there were primarily concerned over your safety because of the presence of the mines that had not been removed from there at that time yet?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they said that the terrain was dangerous, that there were still mines strewn about, and that we, as civilians, should not be there, that it was an area that only the army was controlling and clearing up and that they would not want to leave us there because they wouldn't want to be held responsible for any consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this, of course, pertained to that area within the vicinity of the Vukovar Hospital itself?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to your interview, please. You didn't ask a single question in your interview based on what you experienced in Vukovar on that day, which must have caused you a great impression, everything that you saw in Vukovar, but you never intended to tackle that in your interview, did you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that the pathologists from the military medical academy in Vukovar were also processing, is it were, the bodies at the time, that they were very busy examining the dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was precisely the reason why we didn't cover that subject. There had been a lot of speculation, a lot of unreliable information concerning the victims, and their origin. A professional military team, forensic experts were sent out to examine the bodies and we just wanted to wait and see what the results would be of the work carried out about these professionals.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the interview itself, you said so yesterday, I suppose. You were taking notes, weren't you? You think that even an audio recording was done, but you're not sure about it, are you? The OTP asked you about the Radic interview, and you said that the Sljivancanin interview started at about 2200 hours. Do you remember how long it went on for?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It took quite some time. Several hours, perhaps. I can't be more specific. Two hours, perhaps more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, what strikes me as obvious then, is that not everything that you were talking about was eventually published. You made a selection, as it were, of what you thought would attract the greatest possible interest from your readership, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say there was a photographer there, and another fellow journalist during the interview. Who were these people, who was this other fellow journalist that was there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it was Dragan Vlahovic, who was deputy editor-in-chief at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the same team that had just arrived from Vukovar, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You came together and you left together, the three of you, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you now what my client claims, I'll try to jog your memory about some details of the interview. Do you now remember what Dragan Vlahovic said at the time? Didn't he ask Sljivancanin why they hadn't just chucked him into the Vuka River, in reference to the ICRC man? Do you remember the conversation taking that course?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that now, yes. There were casual remarks like that being made, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now for something else. The OTP asked you whether Sljivancanin made any observations later on when you met. Do you perhaps remember Sljivancanin being particularly unhappy about certain portions of the text, specifically the head line calling him the Knight of Vukovar? Did he complain to Vlahovic about this? Did Vlahovic then in fact offer for a new interview to be put together which Sljivancanin refused because the original one had been published by this time. Do you know anything about this, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is more or less what transpired between the two of them. Sljivancanin believed that this was blown out of proportion, but eventually it stayed this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was because the interview had to be published so soon that no copy was of submitted to Sljivancanin for authorisation prior to the interview being published, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you still have your notes of this interview? Do you still keep any of the tapes that were made? Can these still be found in the archives unit of your former newspaper?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of these have been preserved, regrettably. The newspaper is no longer around, so the archive is gone as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My understanding is you took notes at the time and then you typed the interview up. Since you had to glean from your notes what the conversation actually was, you were in no position to repeat verbatim what your co-locutor [phoen] had told you, had shared with you, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In actual fact, or rather would I be wrong to say that the interview represents your own interpretation of what the interviewee actually said?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I still hope that it was a faithful, accurate interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did say so to the OTP. Was anything said during the interview about how the ICRC man and Sljivancanin got on after this clash at the bridge? Specifically, did Sljivancanin tell you anything about Nicholas Borsinger coming to visit him at Negoslavci the next day to smooth things over, as it were. Do you remember anything being said about that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but nothing -- no great detail was provided about their further contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It seems I will be able to wrap up sooner than I thought. I just have a couple of questions to go. You told the Prosecutor that you later met my client on several different occasions. I expect that you followed at the time what my client was saying to other media and other newspapers after his return from Vukovar, did you not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I follow? Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you then confirm this: Whenever he spoke out in public he always made sure everybody understood he was a man of pro-Yugoslav orientation, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it wasn't quite the "in" thing anymore in any part of Yugoslavia, with the possible exception of some smaller marginal groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He would always speak about the need to preserve Yugoslavia as a whole, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whenever he could he highlighted the multi-ethnic make-up of the JNA, indicating that the JNA was the only multi-ethnic force left in Yugoslavia at the time, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Major Sljivancanin was a staunch believer in the fact that the army was important and the mission of the army was to preserve peace in its own territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked whether the JNA, according to Major Sljivancanin, was the only regular army in Yugoslavia at the time. You heard my question, and I think you answered during one of your previous answers, but can you just confirm that for me, sir, please?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. We will now adjourn and resume at a quarter to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just a few questions in re-examination. But before I start I would like to raise a matter under Rule 90 (H)(ii) in relation to -- especially in relation to the counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin and whether or not the case has been fully put to this witness. What I would ask from the Defence counsel is that if any other aspects of the interview have been disagreed by the accused, Mr. Sljivancanin, that that be put to the witness, there's been a few -- a few aspects being put that has been disagreed by the accused, but the remaining of the interview, the Prosecution would be relying on as accurate. So I'm just calling on my friend, if he disagrees with any other part, I would ask that that be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That is the only matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is being advanced, Mr. Lukic, as I understand it is, whereas you have, in your questioning of the witness got him to agree that he doesn't suggest that the article is verbatim, the words of your client, and nevertheless you have not challenged the specific correctness of any particular parts of it. And if it is your case that they wrongly represent your client's position, that ought to be put to this witness so there can be no doubt. So you know your case. If there is reason to question the accuracy of a particular part in a way that's your material to your case, it would be appropriate for you to put that directly to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I fully understand what my duty is under Rule 90 (H). Also respecting this myself, and Mr. Smith even told me that he would be raising the issue. I have a very human explanation to offer of my position, and of my client's position. First of all, I think that in -- on page 36, paragraph 1 I have asked several questions about the way this interview was done. And I drew the witness's attention to that. When I spoke to Mr. Sljivancanin about the substance of this interview, he simply told me that there were portions that, after all these years, he simply could no longer remember. And I presented my client's position on the relevant page. It's very difficult for me to be putting my case differently, since my client simply doesn't remember some of the things he -- he said 15 years ago. And my question had that sort of general drift.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it clearly from what you have said, Mr. Lukic, that you considered the issue carefully and you believe you have cross-examined as much as you can and should on that issue. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, I will just ask you a few questions that have arisen out of the cross-examination with the Defence. And my first question is about Mr. Sljivancanin and his views on the Yugoslavian state back in 1991. When you spoke to him on the 24th of November, was that the only time that you spoke to him in matters of substance, such as his views on the Yugoslavian state and other matters?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We had no previous opportunities to talk about that, but even later our conversations were not particularly specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You responded to my friend's questions that as far as you can remember you believe that he may have had a negative attitude towards Josip Tito, who was the president of Yugoslavia for many years. How did you get that impression?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that. I can't say whether his impression was negative or not. My view is that he, in fact, did not hold a negative view of Tito, but there is no way I can tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, there may have been a problem in the transcript in relation to that, so that that's now cleared up. Thank you. You were asked by the Defence counsel that the interview that you recorded with Mr. Sljivancanin was your interpretation of what he said in relation to the substance of what he said do you believe that you recorded that accurately or not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If we can go back now to the 24th of November when you went to Vukovar, you said that you were stopped at a check-point at Sid, and then you picked up Mr. Radak, I think on the outskirts of Vukovar, and then you proceeded into Vukovar and you weren't stopped at any check-point. Do you remember say that in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether you passed any check-points as you moved from the outskirts of the town to the centre of the town, even if you weren't stopped?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. If there were any such check-points that we passed on our way, I don't remember any.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In relation to Sasa Radak who escorted you around the town and you said was the commander of the -- sorry, not the commander, but in the death platoon in Vukovar during the conflict, did he seem to be a well-known character around the town when he was relating to other soldiers on that day or when he was relating to anyone or not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really say whether he was a well-known character or not, but he certainly knew his way around Vukovar. He was familiar with all the streets, especially given the fact how difficult it was to get through on account of all the ruins and all the destruction strewn about the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. You described seeing the number of bodies in the medical centre, or in the place that was near the hospital and in the yard. And you've also stated that the soldiers there said that the ethnicity of those bodies was Serbian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I think it was also stated in the article that these soldiers said that they were killed by Ustashas, these victims.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't in my article, but this manufactures did appear in another article which was published in the same issue of our newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you ever able to verify whether, in fact, the victims were Serbian, Croatian, or of any other ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never saw any inconvertible evidence as to the background of the victims. Or about who had killed them or who was to blame that these people had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So the source of that information was from the JNA soldiers that were present where the bodies were; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You were asked a number of questions about, perhaps, your knowledge and the public perception of what had occurred in Vukovar during that three months and the types of topics that you had been asked about in cross-examination by all three counsel are topics such as what was the reason for the JNA and other forces being there, being at Vukovar, you were asked what was the -- were there any atrocities committed by Croats in Vukovar. You were also asked about questions about killings of civilians, Serb civilians in Gospic, a town near Vukovar, and you were also asked about questions relating to the defence of the town, and your knowledge of, say, the Croatian defence of the town. I'd like to clarify the basis of your knowledge. Most -- in relation to your firsthand knowledge of what occurred in Vukovar, obviously you went there on the 24th of November. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you hadn't spoken to anyone from Vukovar, say, a refugee or soldiers that were in Vukovar prior to going on the 24th of November; is that correct? Or had you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is too leading a question. The witness could simply be asked, "Did you talk to anyone? Who was it you talked to?" But this amounts to leading the witness, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I can approach it that way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, I hadn't really seen the problem. I was just going back over that very, very lengthy question, but apart from the length, I hadn't seen the problem. But if you can rephrase it in a way that makes Mr. Lukic happy, that would be wonderful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, you received firsthand knowledge from Captain Radic and Major Sljivancanin on what their role was in Vukovar. Had you received any firsthand knowledge from people involved in the events of Vukovar prior to going there on the 24th of November?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to going there my knowledge was based on information coming from the so-called information centre in Belgrade where documents were being gathered about events in the Vukovar area. Not just Vukovar, but also the surrounding area where there had been combat.
