The statements were collected from refugees and witnesses, all those who came to give evidence about what exactly had gone on. So this was the extent of my firsthand information, as you put it. I spent a lot of time at the centre, I would go through people's statements and sometimes I met some of the people who provided statements. That was all the firsthand knowledge that I had. Everything else was based on media reports and other such sources. When I met Captain Radic and when I met Sljivancanin I tried to give their story in my articles. There is nothing that I learned from them at the time that wasn't published.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And this information centre, it was run by -- run by the Serbian government at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was an NGO. They worked independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you read some of those statements before you went to Vukovar, or was this afterwards?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both before and after. I also heard some testimony from people before I ever went to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you mentioned that there was public perception or you learned that there were atrocities committed by Croats in Vukovar during the fighting. Did you read that in statements or was that from the media, from articles in the media?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was some of that in the media too, but it was mostly based on the accounts of refugees that I learned about what had been going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what specific -- what specific events, what specific atrocities did you hear about in Vukovar from these statements? Are you able to remember or not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to be very specific, but generally speaking people were talking about being expelled from their homes, night-time executions, whole families being taken away from their houses, people who later went missing and were never again found.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you -- did you hear about some of this information through the press?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was there a substantial amount of this information coming from the press?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to say whether it was a substantial amount, but there was quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I think it's your evidence in cross-examination that certainly back in 1991 and during the fighting in Vukovar, that the press was heavily controlled by the state?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The press was under the control of the state, but I don't know about heavily controlled. There was a thing or two that escaped their attention, the attention of the powers that be, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You referred to the way in which the state would control the press, and you referred to that they would place people in key positions in their editorial staff, or positions such as editor-in-chief. Was that happening at the time, people that were pro-Milosevic would have been placed in those positions at the time in the major papers?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was that one of the reasons why you left Politika in 1989, because of the state control of the press, or was it something else, if you can explain?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other reasons too, but this was the preponderant reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In relation to how the state controlled the press at that time, did they -- how did they control it; in terms of the substance that was published, in terms of the style, how they were published? Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't really that specific, it didn't go all the way down to the nitty gritty, not trying to influence somebody's style of writing. But certain topics were imposed and certain others were deliberately neglected or put on the back burner, as it were. Sometimes journalists would prepare an article that didn't pander sufficiently to the needs of the powers that be. Such journalists always put their jobs on the line when doing this, although this was not that frequently the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how did this influence of the state on the media, how did it affect the objectivity of the papers being produced at the time in terms of stating the truth of events?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking there was a school of journalism at the time that had reasonably high standards, and these standards had to be satisfied in order for anything at all to get published. It wasn't a simple matter to impose control, and wherever a control was imposed, it had to be done in a way that was not overly conspicuous, so as to avoid possible resistance and unfavourable reactions from the public itself. There had to be some semblance of objectivity. Now, if we look at how objective certain specific articles or features were, well, all you can say is that in the last instance this very much depended on the specific journalist, and the specific editor in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: At that time, in 1991, say for example if there was reports of atrocities committed by Serb forces against Croat civilians, would that be likely to be published in the paper in relation to this state control you talk about?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose if anything it would be less likely for something like that to be published. Unlike the case for example if a crime had been committed by the other sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So in that sense, the public perceptions were moulded by the -- obviously the journalists, and also by state policy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you able to read any of the Croatian papers being produced at the time, say in late 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In those Croatian papers were they publicising stories and relating to atrocities committed by Croatian soldiers against Serb civilians in Vukovar, did you see stories like that in the Croatian papers?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you able to make a comparison between -- talking about public perceptions now and the ability for the public perception to be accurate, are you able to say what the public perception was of Croatians in -- in Zagreb, in that area, relative to Belgrade, as to what happened in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't think I understand your question. Can you please repeat that for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you aware of the public perception in Croatia, say in Zagreb, was that the same as the public perception that was held in Belgrade, in relation to atrocities committed by Croats against Serbs? Or are you not able to say?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can't say with certainty, but at least as far as I remember my impression at the time was that the Croatian public had no knowledge of any atrocities committed against Serbs in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that the truth of matters in relation to what happened in Vukovar is probably less likely to be found in the papers than from firsthand knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could put it that way. But firsthand knowledge was nearly unavailable to the general public. All the general public had to rely on was the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you mentioned to my friend in cross-examination about the killing of 40 children in an orphanage, and what more do you know about that, and where is that meant to have happened?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this piece of news was broken by one of the foreign agencies, Reuters, I think, and that's why it enjoyed even more credibility at the time. It was about something that was discovered in the Vukovar area, but that's about everything I remember about it. This was later denied and the authenticity of the whole story was challenged. I do remember that there was an Italian journalist who was involved, but that's about the extent of my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you also remember whether a Serb journalist was releasing that story to the television and to the press as well, a young Serb journalist?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember these details. It's possible. It's just that I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In any event, this story that was published in the paper has never been proven to be a fact; is that correct? As far as you are aware.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, the story was subject to much challenging. It was denied on a number of occasions, but never sufficiently disproven as to be generally accepted as not being authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in relation to the statements that you read in Belgrade, the statements that you read in relation to people going missing and executions, were they from -- primarily from Serb refugees returning from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB KACAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part from Serb refugees, yes. To a lesser extent also people of other ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I just have one matter to raise. It's about a couple of corrections to the transcript from previous days. It would only take, I say a minute to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps while the witness is here, that would be good.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not in relation to this witness, it's in relation to other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps in fairness to the witness then, we should conclude his participation. Mr. Kacarevic, you will be pleased to know that that ends your questioning. The Chamber would like very much to thank you for your attendance and for the assistance that you have given. And you are now of course free to return to your home and work. Thank you, indeed. The court officer will show you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian will deal with this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Like Mr. Smith announced, we have two small applications to make. And to assist the Chamber and the parties we have some documents to pass around. And maybe we should wait for the usher to be right back or maybe the registry can assist us on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the registry officer may be able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, you're going to find two small documents in this bundle that was just distributed. The first one -- well, actually we should perhaps go into private session for these two applications, since they deal with protected witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the indication that we are in the position that there is no witness available for the balance of today, we will adjourn now to resume on Monday afternoon at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 10th day of April, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.30 p.m.,
